questions.q: You have fifteen minutes with the leadership team on Friday. What should you write down before building any slide?
options: The list of features to show
The architecture diagram of the solution
The one decision you want at the end of the meeting
The questions you hope nobody asks
questions.why: A demo is a meeting with a purpose, so it is planned backwards from the decision you need.

questions.q: Your demo runs perfectly on every case you picked. Why should you also show a case where the solution is wrong?
options: It builds trust by showing you know where it fails and how the workflow catches it
To lower expectations so the pilot looks better later
Because the leadership team needs to see the error messages
To prove the eval set has enough cases
questions.why: Everyone knows AI makes mistakes; showing you understand them earns more trust than a perfect run.

questions.q: During the demo the sponsor asks, 'Can it also do purchase orders?' It cannot today. What do you do?
options: Say yes and promise it for next month
Say it is easy and show a quick prompt change live
Ignore it and move on to keep to time
Say honestly what it does today, ask what problem that would solve and note it as a backlog candidate
questions.why: Never promise features on the spot; the underlying problem may point to a better next step.

questions.q: The client's team calls them 'exceptions' and 'the AP queue'. How should you refer to them in the demo?
options: Use correct technical terms like edge cases and pipeline
Use their words: exceptions and the AP queue
Mix both so everyone learns the technical terms
Avoid naming them at all
questions.why: Using the client's words keeps the story about their problem, not your tools.

questions.q: The audience heard 'it is 90 percent accurate', but the eval set had only 30 cases. Where do you correct this?
options: Nowhere; a high number helps the project move forward
In the same-day written follow-up that states what was shown, the limits and the next step
In the final hand-over pack months later
Only if someone asks about it
questions.why: The follow-up note is read by people who were not there and stops the story growing in the retelling.

questions.q: After a good POC, the client asks to switch it on for everyone next month. What is the best reply?
options: Agree, since the POC already proved it works
Refuse, since POCs should never move forward
Agree, but only if you stay on to run it
Explain that a pilot with real users comes next, and list what must change before production
questions.why: A POC proves feasibility; value, usability and reliability at volume still need to be proven.

questions.q: What does a pilot prove that a POC does not?
options: Value and usability in real daily work with a small group, and that the review step works
That the technology can work at all on real cases
That the system is reliable at full volume for everyone
That the eval set has enough edge cases
questions.why: The POC proves feasibility; the pilot tests value and usability with real users and a person reviewing.

questions.q: Why agree exit criteria for a pilot before it starts?
options: So the pilot can run as long as needed without pressure
So the FDE can adjust the targets once results come in
So the decision to move on, rerun or stop is judged against measures set in advance, not after seeing results
Because IT requires it before approving sign-in
questions.why: Without written criteria a pilot can drag on with no clear decision.

questions.q: A POC shows the client's data is too poor for the use case. How should you present this?
options: As a failure to hide until a better model appears
As a reason to start the pilot anyway
As a minor issue the production team can fix later
As a valid result that saved the client from a larger failed project, with what was learned
questions.why: Stopping is a valid outcome and should be stated plainly with the lessons recorded.

questions.q: Near the end of a pilot, the FDE still runs the system and owns the success measures. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing; the FDE should own everything until production ends
Ownership should already be shifting to a client business owner, or the solution will depend on the FDE forever
The IT team should own the success measures
The pilot users should own the running system
questions.why: In the pilot a client business owner should own the success measures, with full ownership moving to the client in production.

questions.q: Which of these is an outcome rather than an output?
options: A mailbox connector
A weekly report screen
Clerks no longer download invoices by hand
A confidence score field on each match
questions.why: An outcome is a change in the business; outputs are the things you build to get there.

questions.q: After the first demo, finance, support and supply chain all ask for new features by next month. How do you choose what to build?
options: Tie each request to an outcome, score value with the client and effort with the builders, and rank them
Build what the most senior person asked for
Build the requests in the order they arrived
Build the hardest item first to show capability
questions.why: An outcome-tied, ranked backlog lets you say yes and no with reasons the client agrees with.

questions.q: A backlog item scores high value and high effort. What do you do with it?
options: Plan it and break it into smaller pieces
Do it first, before anything else
Park it and tell the requester why
Do it only when there is spare time
questions.why: High value, high effort items are worth doing but need splitting into pieces that finish in days.

questions.q: You start a pilot that aims to cut invoice handling time, but you never recorded handling time beforehand. What is the problem?
options: Handling time is a lagging measure and should not be used
The pilot should measure eval pass rate only
Without a baseline you cannot show the pilot improved anything
Baselines are only needed in production
questions.why: You must measure the starting point before changing anything, or improvement cannot be shown.

questions.q: Single sign-on scores only medium value and medium effort, but IT review requires it. How should you treat it?
options: Park it, because the score is not high enough
Plan it anyway; some items are needed regardless of score
Drop it, because it does not serve an outcome
Ask the client to raise its value score so it ranks first
questions.why: The value versus effort score is a conversation tool, and required items still have to be done.

questions.q: The client asks who they call when it breaks after you leave. Which three parts must the hand-over pack contain?
options: The source code, a slide deck and a final invoice
An eval set, a roadmap and a demo recording
A RACI, an architecture diagram and the API keys
A runbook, a named owner and a support model
questions.why: These three let the client operate the system, own the outcome and route problems without you.

questions.q: A draft RACI lists 'the IT team' as Accountable for approving releases. What should you change?
options: Add the FDE as a second Accountable
Move IT to Informed and leave Accountable empty
Name one person as Accountable for that task
Nothing; a team is fine as Accountable
questions.why: Only one named person should be Accountable per task, or everyone assumes someone else will handle it.

questions.q: When writing the common problems section of a runbook, how should each row start?
options: From the technical root cause
From the name of the code file involved
From the date the problem first happened
From the symptom a person notices, then the first check and the fix or escalation
questions.why: Problems are reported by what people notice, so support teams look them up by symptom.

questions.q: The runbook needs to explain where the LLM API key lives. What should it contain?
options: The name of the secret and where it is stored, never its value
The key value, so the support team can rotate it fast
Nothing about secrets, for security reasons
A screenshot of the key in the cloud console
questions.why: The next owner needs to find the secret, but putting its value in a document leaks it.

questions.q: How do you know the hand-over has worked?
options: The client has signed the final invoice
The owner can do a routine check and a rollback without your help, and the client owns every account and key
The runbook is longer than ten pages
You are still on call to fix any issue
questions.why: If the client team can run it alone and holds all access, the system no longer depends on you.
